summary: Describes the architecture of WHOIS++, an extension of the simple WHOIS service in RFC 954 that lets WHOIS-like servers offer more structured information. It was standards-track but is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: WHOIS++ defines a way to search structured records held by many directory servers. Index servers summarize what other servers contain and help direct searches to likely matches.

subtitle: A distributed directory protocol that adds structured records, richer searches and server indexing to WHOIS.

tldr.problem: The original WHOIS stored mostly unstructured records and relied on a simple query to one server. The RFC says that design could not provide a reliable, Internet-wide directory.
tldr.mechanism: WHOIS++ gives records defined templates, adds search constraints and Boolean expressions, and lets index servers collect summaries from other servers to direct queries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1835 is Historic. It specifies both the lookup protocol and an extensible model for connecting directory servers.

today: RFC 1835 is Historic. It specifies a structured directory protocol with searches across servers through index information.

sections.title: Why Extend WHOIS
sections.content:
The RFC describes the earlier WHOIS service as a simple directory for a limited set of users. Its records were text with little structure, and searches matched strings or record handles. As more services appeared, their additions were made in an uncoordinated way.

A single server could not guarantee the response and reliability expected of a large directory. WHOIS++ therefore extends the data model and query protocol while leaving each server free to choose its own storage and search engine.
sections.plainLanguage: The original WHOIS had simple text records and basic searches. WHOIS++ adds a shared structure and connects separate servers, so one lookup service does not have to hold every record.

sections.title: Templates and Record Handles
sections.content:
A WHOIS++ record contains ordered attribute and value pairs and follows a template. A template specifies the record type and its fields, such as a person or service record. Records have unique handles, and each database also has a unique server handle.

A client can limit a search by template type, attribute, value or handle. This structure makes records easier for software to parse while keeping replies readable to people.
sections.plainLanguage: A template sets the fields used by a kind of record. A record has its own handle, and its server has a separate handle, so searches can identify both the information and its source.

sections.title: Base Servers and Index Servers
sections.content:
A base-level server contains completed records. An index server holds pointers to other servers and forward knowledge about the records they contain. A single physical server may perform both roles.

One form of forward knowledge is a centroid: a summary of the templates, attributes and values represented by a server's records. An index server collects this information and can direct a query to servers that may contain matching records. Index servers can also point to other index servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Base servers hold records. Index servers collect summaries and pointers, then direct a search toward servers that may have matching information.

sections.title: Searches, Constraints and Replies
sections.content:
A search combines one or more terms. Terms can be joined with AND, OR and NOT, and parentheses can change how the server groups them. Required constraints select a search method, response format and maximum number of matches. Optional constraints can control language, character set, authentication and which attributes appear in a reply.

The five response formats are FULL, ABRIDGED, HANDLE, SUMMARY and SERVER-TO-ASK. The last format points to other servers that may answer a query; conforming servers are required to support the first four formats.
sections.plainLanguage: You can combine search terms and ask for full records, brief results, handles or a match summary. An index server can also return pointers to other servers that may have an answer.

sections.title: Authentication and Unencrypted Data
sections.content:
WHOIS++ is designed as a simple information lookup service, but the RFC also describes optional authentication for a transaction. Its named method sends a username and password with the search string.

The RFC warns that this method does not encrypt either the password or the information sent over the network. It leaves the choice of what information to expose, and how to protect it, to the people operating a service.
sections.plainLanguage: The optional password method does not hide the password or search information while they travel across the network. Service operators must decide what information to make available.
